method: Altitude oxygen turns an elevation into the pressure of the air, then into the oxygen pressure a breath delivers. Standard station pressure follows the International Standard Atmosphere: p = 1013.25 hPa x (1 - 2.25577e-5 x h)^5.25588, with h in metres, a sea-level temperature of 15 C and a 6.5 C/km lapse rate, the tropospheric model valid to 11 km. The page accepts elevations from -500 to 9,000 m and converts feet with 1 ft = 0.3048 m. Inspired oxygen pressure is FiO2 x (p - 6.266 kPa), with FiO2 = 0.20946 and 6.266 kPa the saturated water-vapour pressure of air at 37 C; it is reported in kPa and mmHg (1 kPa = 7.50062 mmHg). Oxygen availability divides that value by its sea-level result of 19.91 kPa, so sea level is exactly 100% and elevations below sea level are above it. An optional measured station pressure from 300 to 1100 hPa replaces the standard value, and the pressure altitude is the standard-atmosphere altitude that would produce the pressure in use, obtained by inverting the same formula. A caution is raised when the elevation is 2,500 m or more, when a measured pressure differs from the standard atmosphere by more than 3%, and when the elevation is below sea level. Display is rounded: pressure to 0.1 hPa, inspired oxygen to 0.01 kPa and 0.1 mmHg, availability and pressure ratio to 0.1%, altitudes to the nearest metre and foot, with calculations in double precision. The reference table lists the standard atmosphere every 500 m from 0 to 5,000 m. The standard atmosphere is a reference model rather than a weather report, so real station pressure varies by a few percent with weather and temperature and humidity shift density further. The result is physics, not a medical measurement: it does not predict altitude illness, acclimatisation, oxygen saturation or performance. Everything runs in the browser with no network access, uploads or storage.

sources.title: International Civil Aviation Organization, Manual of the ICAO Standard Atmosphere, Doc 7488/3 (1993): sea-level pressure 1013.25 hPa, 15 C, a 6.5 C/km tropospheric lapse rate and the barometric formula used here.
U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976 (NASA TM-X-74335 and NOAA-S/T 76-1562): the same tropospheric model, its 5.25588 exponent and its valid range to 11 km.
West, J. B., Respiratory Physiology: The Essentials, 9th edition: inspired oxygen pressure is FiO2 x (PB - PH2O), with PH2O about 47 mmHg (6.27 kPa) at 37 C and FiO2 about 0.2095 in dry air.
